items.title: Volume and surface area
items.content: Cube: \(V=a^3, TSA=6a^2, LSA=4a^2\). Cuboid: \(V=lbh, TSA=2(lb+bh+hl)\). Cylinder: \(V=\pi r^2h, CSA=2\pi rh, TSA=2\pi r(h+r)\).

items.title: Units and capacity
items.content: Volume uses cubic units. \(1\,\mathrm{cm}^3=1\,\mathrm{mL}\), \(1000\,\mathrm{cm}^3=1\,\mathrm L\), and \(1\,\mathrm m^3=1000\,\mathrm L\). Use consistent units before calculating.

items.title: Exam checks
items.content:
Sketch and label all dimensions before choosing a formula.
For recasting, conserve volume rather than surface area.

items.title: Cone, sphere and hemisphere formulas
items.content: Cone: (V= rac13pi r^2h), slant height (l=sqrt{r^2+h^2}), curved area (=pi rl), total area (=pi r(l+r)). Sphere: (V= rac43pi r^3), area (=4pi r^2). Hemisphere: (V= rac23pi r^3), curved area (=2pi r^2), total area (=3pi r^2).

items.title: Cube and cuboid
items.content: Worked example: cuboid 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm has volume 120 cm³ and total surface area \(2(40+15+24)=158\) cm².

items.title: Cylinder
items.content: Worked example: radius 7 cm, height 10 cm. Volume \(=\pi(49)(10)=1540\) cm³ using \(22/7\); curved area \(=2\pi(7)(10)=440\) cm².

items.title: Identify exposed surface
items.content: Total surface area includes all faces; lateral/curved area excludes end faces. A closed box and an open-top box need different area totals. Worked example: an open cuboid omits the top face lb from its closed-box surface area.

items.title: Capacity and liquid
items.content: Worked example: a tank of 2 m³ holds \(2000\) L. Convert cubic units before comparing capacity.

items.title: Composite solids and melting/recasting
items.content: For joined solids add volumes if they do not overlap. When a solid is recast without loss, total volume is conserved; surface area can change. Worked example: 300 cm³ of metal cast into 25 cm³ pieces makes 300/25 = 12 pieces.

items.title: Scale effects
items.content: If every length is multiplied by \(k\), surface area scales by \(k^2\), volume by \(k^3\). Worked example: doubling a cube’s side multiplies its volume by 2³ = 8.

items.title: Cone
items.content: Worked example: (r=3) cm and (h=4) cm give (l=5) cm. Volume (= rac13pi(9)(4)=12pi) cm³; curved surface area (=pi(3)(5)=15pi) cm².

items.title: Sphere and hemisphere
items.content: Worked example: a sphere of radius 3 cm has volume ( rac43pi(27)=36pi) cm³ and surface area (4pi(9)=36pi) cm². A hemisphere’s total area includes its circular base.

items.title: Find volume or surface area
items.content: Worked example: cube side 4 cm gives volume 64 cm³ and total surface area 96 cm².

items.title: Find a missing dimension
items.content: Use the given volume and isolate the unknown. Worked example: cuboid volume 180 cm³, length 9 cm, breadth 5 cm gives height \(180/(45)=4\) cm.

items.title: Capacity or fill problem
items.content: Calculate the container volume, convert to litres/millilitres, then compare with the liquid amount. Worked example: a 50 cm × 40 cm × 30 cm tank holds 60,000 cm³ = 60 L.

items.title: Open or closed container
items.content: Count only exposed faces; an open-top cuboid omits the top rectangle. Worked example: an open box with l=5, b=4, h=3 has exposed area lb + 2lh + 2bh = 74 cm².

items.title: Recasting or combining solids
items.content: Conserve volume under melting/recasting; add or subtract volumes for composite solids. Worked example: a 216 cm³ cube recast into 27 cm³ spheres makes 216/27 = 8 spheres.

items.title: Cone or sphere calculation
items.content: Select the formula from the solid and requested measure. Worked example: a hemisphere with (r=3) cm has curved area (2pi r^2=18pi) cm² and total area (3pi r^2=27pi) cm².

items.title: Derive cuboid volume
items.content: A layer has base area \(lb\). Stacking \(h\) unit-depth layers gives \(V=lbh\).

items.title: Derive cuboid surface area
items.content: A cuboid has three pairs of equal rectangles: areas \(lb\), \(bh\), and \(hl\); total is \(2(lb+bh+hl)\).

items.title: Derive cylinder volume
items.content: A cylinder has constant circular cross-section \(\pi r^2\) through height \(h\), so volume is base area × height: \(V=\pi r^2h\).

items.title: Derive cylinder curved surface area
items.content: Unroll the curved surface into a rectangle with length equal to circumference \(2\pi r\) and width \(h\); area is \(2\pi rh\).

items.title: Cone volume relation
items.content: A cone with the same base radius and height as a cylinder has one-third its volume: (V= rac13pi r^2h). Use the cone formula as the standard mensuration result; the factor ( rac13) is essential.

sections.title: Common errors and how to avoid them

items.title: Confusing area and volume units
items.content: Use cm² for area and cm³ for volume.

items.title: Using diameter as radius
items.content: Halve the diameter before applying cylinder formulas.

items.title: Counting hidden faces
items.content: For open or attached solids, count only the surfaces specified as exposed.

items.title: Converting cubic units linearly
items.content: A length conversion is cubed for volume; 1 m³ = 1,000,000 cm³.

items.title: Confusing cone height and slant height
items.content: Volume uses vertical height (h); curved surface area uses slant height (l). For a right cone, (l^2=r^2+h^2).

keyTakeaways: Volume is base area times height for prisms/cylinders.
Cubic-unit conversions involve the cube of the length factor.
Recasting conserves volume when there is no loss.
